## Introduction: The Hidden State {.left auto-animate="true"}

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

::: {.fragment  .fade-in}
### Error is inescapable 
What is 5 cm truely? Can we ever measure a perfect 5cm?
:::
::: {.fragment  .fade-in}
### Yes and No
* To a drill press : 5cm => 5cm +- .5cm
* To a mill : 5cm => 5cm +- .005cm
* To an ASML Photolithography Machine: 5cm => 5cm +- 0.000002cm
:::

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {style="height: 5em;"}
:::
::: {.fragment .goal-box .fade-up}
### Today's Goal
The Mathmatics of finding truth through Error, and incorporating new data as Evidence rather than truth. 
Since by definition we cannot measure the error of any particular measurment, We use probability to model the likelyhood of sensing a true value
:::
::: {style="height: 2em;"}
:::
:::

:::



## Boolean vs. Probabilistic Logic {.compact-slide}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
:::{.fragment}
### Boolean Logic

```python
# Boolean logic example
# if (Shooter_will_make_the_shot == True):
#     shoot
```


:::
:::{.fragment}
### Probabilistic Logic

```python
# Probability logic example
# if (Probability_we_make_the_shot >= 80%)
#     shoot
```

:::

:::
:::{.column width="50%"}
:::{.fragment}
### Key difference:
Combining evidence with trust levels enables better decisions.

* Boolean: Instantaneous sensor read → immediate judgment

* Probabilistic: Averages sensor noise, reduces false positives/negatives

:::
:::{.fragment}
### Caveat:
There are alternative filtering approaches that don't rely on probability:

- Rolling average on distance sensors
- Debounce period on limit switches  
- Moving median filters
- Exponential smoothing
- These can work very well depending on implementation and use case
:::
:::
::::

## Understanding Set Space {auto-animate=true data-autoslide="0"}
:::{.fragment}
- We want a number that represents how often something happens, or does not
:::
:::{.fragment}
- If you know nothing about an event, you could assume it's a 50:50 chance, pass or fail, it will happen or it wont
:::
:::{.fragment}
- With Evidence about the type of event (I.E. Rolling a 2 on a D6 Die) you can refine your guess, in this case to 1:6
:::
:::{.fragment}
- You can also experiment to find probability. If given a weighted die, you could roll it many times to gather data, and hone in on the true likelyhood of any given face landing up. 
:::

### Probability of Hitting The shot GIVEN the evidence the Shooter is broken
Lets define ratios in terms of prior Set "All Possible States: Balls Shot"

::: {.legacy-diagram}

<div data-id="circle2" style="position: absolute; left: 310px; top: 20px; width: 880px; height: 880px; background: rgba(100, 255, 100, 0.22); border: 4px solid #64ff64; border-radius: 50%;"></div>

## Understanding Set Space {auto-animate=true data-autoslide="0"}
### Probability of Hitting The shot GIVEN the evidence the Shooter is broken
So what is P(Target Hit | Shooter was broken)?

::: {.legacy-diagram}

<div data-id="circle2" style="position: absolute; left: 310px; top: 20px; width: 880px; height: 880px; background: rgba(100, 255, 100, 0.22); border: 4px solid #64ff64; border-radius: 50%;"></div>

<div data-id="circle1" style="position: absolute; left: 200px; top: 200px; width: 700px; height: 700px; background: rgba(255, 100, 100, 0.30); border: 4px solid #ff6464; border-radius: 50%;"></div>

<div data-id="label1" style="position: absolute; left: 335px; top: 500px; width: 390px; color: white; font-size: 34px; text-align: center;">$$P(\text{Target Hit} \cap \text{Shooter Broken})$$</div>
<!-- <div data-id="label1prob" style="position: absolute; left: 150px; top: 550px; color: white; font-size: 50px;">P(Target Hit AND Shooter Was Broken)</div> -->

<div data-id="label2" style="position: absolute; left: 760px; top: 70px; color: white; font-size: 34px;">$$P(\text{Shooter Was Broken})$$</div>



<div data-id="eq" style="position: absolute;left: 150px; top: 750px; color: white; font-size: 30px; text-align: center;">
$$P(\text{Target Hit} \mid \text{Shooter Broken}) = \frac{P(\text{Target Hit} \cap \text{Shooter Broken})}{P(\text{Shooter Broken})}$$
</div>

:::
<!-- Slide 5: Understanding Set Space (Part 3 - AND) -->
## Understanding Set Space {auto-animate=true data-autoslide="0"}
### Bayes Theorem

::: {.legacy-diagram}


<div data-id="eq" style="position: absolute;left: 50px; top: 200px; color: white; font-size: 30px; text-align: center; width: 95%;">
$$P(\text{Target Hit} \mid \text{Shooter Broken}) = \frac{P(\text{Target Hit} \cap \text{Shooter Broken})}{P(\text{Shooter Broken})}$$
</div>
<div data-id="eq2" style="position: absolute;left: 50px; top: 350px; color: white; font-size: 30px; text-align: center; width: 95%;">
$$P(\text{Shooter Broken}) = \frac{P(\text{Target Hit} \cap \text{Shooter Broken})}{P(\text{Target Hit} \mid \text{Shooter Broken})}$$
</div>
<div data-id="eq3" style="position: absolute;left: 50px; top: 500px; color: white; font-size: 30px; text-align: center; width: 95%;">
$$P(\text{Target Hit} \cap \text{Shooter Broken}) = P(\text{Shooter Broken}) \times P(\text{Target Hit} \mid \text{Shooter Broken})$$
</div>

:::
<!-- Slide 5: Understanding Set Space (Part 3 - AND) -->
## Understanding Set Space {auto-animate=true data-autoslide="0"}
### Bayes Theorem -- Generally

::: {.legacy-diagram}


<div data-id="eq" style="position: absolute;left: 50px; top: 200px; color: white; font-size: 30px; text-align: center; width: 95%;">
$$P(\text{Event} \mid \text{Evidence}) = \frac{P(\text{Event} \cap \text{Evidence})}{P(\text{Evidence})}$$
</div>
<div data-id="eq2" style="position: absolute;left: 50px; top: 350px; color: white; font-size: 30px; text-align: center; width: 95%;">
$$P(\text{Evidence}) = \frac{P(\text{Event} \cap \text{Evidence})}{P(\text{Event} \mid \text{Evidence})}$$
</div>
<div data-id="eq3" style="position: absolute;left: 50px; top: 500px; color: white; font-size: 30px; text-align: center; width: 95%;">
$$P(\text{Event} \cap \text{Evidence}) = P(\text{Evidence}) \times P(\text{Event} \mid \text{Evidence})$$
</div>

:::
<!-- Slide 5: Understanding Set Space (Part 3 - AND) -->
## Understanding Set Space {.dense-diagram auto-animate=true data-autoslide="0"}
### Bayes Theorem -- Generally
For events that are dependent, finding The intersection (AND) can be difficult. So Bayes tells us =>

::: {.legacy-diagram}



<div data-id="eq3" style="position: absolute;left: 50px; top: 100px; color: white; font-size: 30px; text-align: center; width: 95%;">
$$P(\text{Evidence} \cap \text{Event}) = P(\text{Event}) \times P(\text{Evidence} \mid \text{Event})$$
</div>
<div data-id="eqtext" style="position: absolute;left: 50px; top: 300px; color: white; font-size: 60px; text-align: center; width: 95%;">
So we substitute and rewrite the our original equation as:
</div>

<div data-id="eq4" style="position: absolute;left: 50px; top: 500px; color: white; font-size: 30px; text-align: center; width: 95%;">
$$P(\text{Event} \mid \text{Evidence}) = \frac{P(\text{Event}) \times P(\text{Evidence} \mid \text{Event})}{P(\text{Evidence})}$$
</div>


:::

<!-- Slide 5: Understanding Set Space (Part 3 - AND) -->
## Understanding Set Space {.compact-slide auto-animate=true data-autoslide="0"}
### Bayes Theorem — Evidence Accumulates

For dependent events, Bayes gives us a practical way to update a belief with new evidence:

$$
P(\text{Event} \mid \text{Evidence})
=
\frac{P(\text{Event})\,P(\text{Evidence} \mid \text{Event})}{P(\text{Evidence})}
$$

::: {.evidence-flow}

::: {.evidence-card}
**1. Start with a prior**
Our confidence before the new observation.
:::

::: {.evidence-card}
**2. Evaluate the evidence**
Ask how likely this observation is under the event.
:::

::: {.evidence-card}
**3. Calculate the posterior**
The updated confidence after incorporating the evidence.
:::

::: {.evidence-card}
**4. Repeat**
Use the posterior as the prior for the next observation.
:::

:::

::: {.highlight-box}
Reliable evidence strengthens confidence; contradictory evidence weakens it. Repeating the loop produces increasingly informed beliefs.
:::

## Activity — Diagnose the Hidden Motor {#activity-setup .compact-slide}

### The question

One box was chosen and stays hidden. Each bead is a new test result. **Which motor is more likely?**

::: {.activity-grid}
::: {.activity-card .good-motor}
**Hypothesis A — motor is good**

**90% green** · **10% red**

A red result is unusual when the motor is healthy.
:::

::: {.activity-card .bad-motor}
**Hypothesis B — motor is broken**

**50% green** · **50% red**

A red result is five times more likely when it is broken.
:::
:::

::: {.prior-strip}
<span><strong>Starting prior:</strong> no preference yet</span>
<span class="prior-value good">Good 50%</span>
<span class="prior-value bad">Broken 50%</span>
:::

::: {.presenter-prompt}
**Ask the room:** If the first test is red, which hypothesis should gain confidence—and why?
:::

## Test 1 — A Red Result {#activity-test-one .compact-slide}

### Step 1: weight each hypothesis by how well it predicts red

::: {.bayes-weights}
::: {.weight-card}
**Good motor**
Prior × likelihood<br>
$0.50 \times 0.10 = 0.05$
:::

::: {.weight-card .emphasis}
**Broken motor**
Prior × likelihood<br>
$0.50 \times 0.50 = 0.25$
:::
:::

### Step 2: normalize the two weights

$$
P(\text{Broken}\mid\text{Red})
=\frac{0.25}{0.05+0.25}
=\mathbf{83.3\%}
$$

<div class="belief-bar" role="img" aria-label="Posterior probability: good motor 16.7 percent, broken motor 83.3 percent.">
  <span class="belief-good" style="width: 16.7%;">Good 16.7%</span><span class="belief-bad" style="width: 83.3%;">Broken 83.3%</span>
</div>

::: {.highlight-box}
The **posterior is 83.3% broken**. That posterior becomes the prior for the next test.
:::

## Test Again — A Green Result {#activity-test-two .compact-slide}

### Step 3: reuse the posterior as the new prior

::: {.update-chain}
<span>Previous posterior</span><strong>83.3% broken</strong><span class="flow-arrow">→</span><span>New prior</span><strong>83.3% broken</strong>
:::

### Step 4: apply the green likelihoods

::: {.bayes-weights}
::: {.weight-card}
**Good motor**
$0.167 \times 0.90 = 0.150$
:::

::: {.weight-card .emphasis}
**Broken motor**
$0.833 \times 0.50 = 0.417$
:::
:::

$$
P(\text{Broken}\mid\text{Red, Green})
=\frac{0.417}{0.150+0.417}
=\mathbf{73.5\%}
$$

<div class="belief-bar" role="img" aria-label="Updated probability: good motor 26.5 percent, broken motor 73.5 percent.">
  <span class="belief-good" style="width: 26.5%;">Good 26.5%</span><span class="belief-bad" style="width: 73.5%;">Broken 73.5%</span>
</div>

::: {.presenter-prompt}
Green is evidence for a good motor, so confidence in “broken” falls—but one green result does not erase the earlier red result.
:::

</div>

<div class="demo-summary">
<div class="draw-result" data-role="draw-result">
<span class="result-ball neutral"></span>
<span><strong>No draws yet</strong><small>Press “Draw a ball” to collect evidence.</small></span>
</div>
<div class="draw-history-wrap">
<strong>Evidence so far</strong>
<div class="draw-history" data-role="history"><span class="empty-history">None yet</span></div>
</div>
</div>

<div class="live-math" aria-live="polite">
<div class="math-stage">
<span class="stage-label">1. Prior</span>
<strong>Broken <span data-role="prior-b">50.0%</span></strong>
<small>Good <span data-role="prior-a">50.0%</span></small>
</div>
<div class="math-operator">×</div>
<div class="math-stage">
<span class="stage-label">2. Likelihood</span>
<strong>P(<span data-role="color-one">result</span> | Broken) = <span data-role="like-b">—</span></strong>
<small>P(<span data-role="color-two">result</span> | Good) = <span data-role="like-a">—</span></small>
</div>
<div class="math-operator">→</div>
<div class="math-stage">
<span class="stage-label">3. Weighted evidence</span>
<strong>Broken: <span data-role="weight-b">—</span></strong>
<small>Good: <span data-role="weight-a">—</span></small>
</div>
<div class="math-operator">→</div>
<div class="math-stage result-stage">
<span class="stage-label">4. New posterior</span>
<strong>Broken <span data-role="posterior-b">50.0%</span></strong>
<small>Becomes the next prior</small>
</div>
</div>

<div class="belief-bar interactive-belief" role="img" data-role="belief-bar" aria-label="Current belief: good motor 50 percent, broken motor 50 percent.">
<span class="belief-good" data-role="bar-a" style="width: 50%;">Good 50.0%</span><span class="belief-bad" data-role="bar-b" style="width: 50%;">Broken 50.0%</span>
</div>

<div class="demo-explanation" data-role="explanation">Every draw uses the current posterior as the next prior. Draw repeatedly and watch the estimate respond.</div>
</div>

## Repeat — Each Test Refines the Estimate {#activity-repeat .compact-slide}

### Example sequence from the same hidden box: Red → Green → Red → Green

| Test | Observation | Prior: broken | Updated belief: broken | Interpretation |
|:--|:--:|--:|--:|:--|
| Start | — | — | **50.0%** | Both hypotheses are equally plausible |
| 1 | Red | 50.0% | **83.3%** | Strong evidence for broken |
| 2 | Green | 83.3% | **73.5%** | Evidence pulls back toward good |
| 3 | Red | 73.5% | **93.3%** | Repeated red makes broken very likely |
| 4 | Green | 93.3% | **88.5%** | Estimate adjusts, but remains confident |

::: {.activity-loop}
<strong>Prior</strong><span>×</span><strong>likelihood of new result</strong><span>→</span><strong>normalize</strong><span>→</span><strong>posterior</strong><span>↻ next test</span>
:::

::: {.highlight-box}
We never “start over.” We carry forward what we learned, then let each new observation correct the estimate. A Kalman filter performs this same cycle with position measurements.
:::

---

## Let's Take a Break {.center}

### When we return

We will turn the same **prior → evidence → posterior** loop into a better estimate of position.

## Two Imperfect Beliefs {.gaussian-slide auto-animate=true auto-animate-easing="ease-in-out"}

<div class="gaussian-canvas" role="img" aria-label="A broad model prediction and a narrower sensor measurement shown as probability distributions.">
  <div class="probability-baseline"></div>
  <div data-id="model-curve" class="distribution model-distribution" style="left: 120px; width: 760px; height: 380px;"></div>
  <div data-id="sensor-curve" class="distribution sensor-distribution" style="left: 900px; width: 420px; height: 520px; opacity: 1;"></div>

  <div data-id="sensor-mean" class="mean-line sensor-mean" style="left: 1110px; height: 530px;"></div>
  <div data-id="model-label" class="curve-label" style="left: 300px;">Prior: model prediction</div>
  <div data-id="sensor-label" class="curve-label" style="left: 990px;">Evidence: sensor reading</div>
</div>

<div class="gaussian-legend">
  <span><i class="legend-swatch model-swatch"></i> Wider curve = less confidence</span>
  <span><i class="legend-swatch sensor-swatch"></i> Narrower curve = more confidence</span>
</div>

## Combine Two Imperfect Guesses {.gaussian-slide auto-animate=true auto-animate-easing="ease-in-out"}

<div class="gaussian-canvas" role="img" aria-label="The model prediction moves toward the more precise sensor measurement and becomes a narrower posterior distribution.">
  <div class="probability-baseline"></div>
  <div data-id="model-curve" class="distribution posterior-distribution" style="left: 710px; width: 500px; height: 570px;"></div>
  <div data-id="sensor-curve" class="distribution sensor-distribution" style="left: 900px; width: 420px; height: 520px; opacity: 0.22;"></div>
  <div data-id="model-mean" class="mean-line posterior-mean" style="left: 960px; height: 580px;"></div>
  <div data-id="sensor-mean" class="mean-line sensor-mean" style="left: 1110px; height: 530px; opacity: 0.22;"></div>
  <div data-id="model-label" class="curve-label posterior-label" style="left: 790px;">Updated best guess</div>
  <div data-id="sensor-label" class="curve-label muted-label" style="left: 1020px; opacity: 0.35;">New sensor reading</div>
</div>

::: {.highlight-box}
The new best guess lands between the prediction and the sensor reading—but closer to whichever one is more dependable. The narrower shape means **we are now more confident**.
:::

---

## A Kalman Filter Is Bayes in Motion

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="48%"}

### Bayes asks one useful question

> “Given my old guess and this new evidence, what is my better guess now?”

::: {.plain-language-card}
**Old guess** + **new evidence** → **updated guess**
:::

:::

::: {.column width="52%"}

### A Kalman filter asks it again and again

- **Old guess:** where motion says the object should be.
- **New evidence:** where a sensor says the object is.
- **Updated guess:** the most believable location right now.
- Then motion carries that answer forward to the next moment.

:::

:::

---

## The Four-Step Loop

<div class="kalman-flow" aria-label="Kalman filter cycle: make a prediction, read the sensor, compare confidence, update the guess, then repeat.">
<div class="flow-card fragment fade-up">
<span class="flow-number">1</span>
<h3>Make a guess</h3>
<p>Use the last position and direction of travel to predict what happens next.</p>
</div>
<div class="flow-arrow" aria-hidden="true">→</div>
<div class="flow-card fragment fade-up">
<span class="flow-number">2</span>
<h3>Read the sensor</h3>
<p>Get a fresh—but imperfect—observation of where the object is.</p>
</div>
<div class="flow-arrow" aria-hidden="true">→</div>
<div class="flow-card fragment fade-up">
<span class="flow-number">3</span>
<h3>Compare confidence</h3>
<p>Ask which source has usually been more dependable.</p>
</div>
<div class="flow-arrow" aria-hidden="true">→</div>
<div class="flow-card fragment fade-up">
<span class="flow-number">4</span>
<h3>Update the guess</h3>
<p>Move toward the sensor by the appropriate amount, then repeat.</p>
</div>
</div>

::: {.takeaway-line}
**Predict where it is going. Check what the sensor saw. Blend them according to trust.**
:::

---

## Motion Fills the Gaps {.motion-gap-slide}

Sensors give us **snapshots**. The object keeps moving between those snapshots.

<div class="motion-timeline" role="img" aria-label="At zero seconds the sensor sees the object at two meters. At one second there is no reading, so motion predicts three meters. At two seconds the sensor sees 4.2 meters and the estimate is corrected.">
<div class="motion-step observed">
<span class="time-label">0 seconds</span>
<span class="timeline-dot"></span>
<strong>Sensor sees 2.0 m</strong>
<small>Start with an observed position</small>
</div>
<div class="timeline-connector"></div>
<div class="motion-step predicted">
<span class="time-label">1 second</span>
<span class="timeline-dot"></span>
<strong>No new reading</strong>
<small>Motion predicts about 3.0 m</small>
</div>
<div class="timeline-connector"></div>
<div class="motion-step corrected">
<span class="time-label">2 seconds</span>
<span class="timeline-dot"></span>
<strong>Sensor sees 4.2 m</strong>
<small>Use it to correct the prediction</small>
</div>
</div>

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}
### Remember only position

“It was at 2.0 m.” The estimate becomes stale as soon as the object moves.
:::

::: {.column width="52%"}
### Remember position and motion

“It was at 2.0 m and moving right.” Now we can make a useful prediction while the sensor is silent.
:::
:::

::: {.takeaway-line}
**Motion carries the estimate forward. The next sensor reading pulls it back toward reality.**
:::

---

## The “Trust Dial” Controls the Move

<div class="gain-grid">
<div class="gain-card">
<span class="gain-value">Dial near 0</span>
<h3>Mostly trust motion</h3>
<p>The sensor is unreliable, so the guess barely moves toward it.</p>
</div>
<div class="gain-card active-gain">
<span class="gain-value">Dial in the middle</span>
<h3>Blend both</h3>
<p>Both sources have value, so the answer lands between them.</p>
</div>
<div class="gain-card">
<span class="gain-value">Dial near 1</span>
<h3>Mostly trust the sensor</h3>
<p>The reading is dependable, so the guess moves close to it.</p>
</div>
</div>

::: {.plain-language-equation}
**Updated guess** = motion prediction + **some fraction of the gap** toward the sensor
:::

Engineers call that fraction the **Kalman gain**. It is calculated from the relative uncertainty of the prediction and the sensor—not chosen by hand each time.

---

## Why the Combination Works Better

<div class="comparison-grid">
<div class="comparison-card">
<span class="comparison-icon">Motion only</span>
<h3>It drifts</h3>
<p>Tiny errors accumulate, so the predicted position slowly wanders away.</p>
</div>
<div class="comparison-card">
<span class="comparison-icon">Sensor only</span>
<h3>It jitters</h3>
<p>Individual readings bounce around, even when the object moves smoothly.</p>
</div>
<div class="comparison-card comparison-best">
<span class="comparison-icon">Kalman filter</span>
<h3>It stays smooth and grounded</h3>
<p>Motion fills the gaps; sensors keep the prediction connected to reality.</p>
</div>
</div>

::: {.highlight-box}
A Kalman filter does not claim to know the exact truth. It keeps a **best guess plus an honest measure of confidence**, then improves both whenever new evidence arrives.
:::

---

## The Big Picture {.center}

<div class="big-picture">

**Prediction**
where motion says it should be

<span aria-hidden="true">+</span>

**Observation**
where the sensor says it is

<span aria-hidden="true">→</span>

**Updated best guess**
where we now think it is—and how sure we are

</div>

### Then repeat at the next time step.

::: {.takeaway-line}
**A Kalman filter is a repeating trust exercise:** predict, observe, blend, and carry the improved guess forward.
:::

---
